L45@P1-2: 11 Introduction
L46@P2: “Between the idea and the reality . . .
L47@P2: falls the shadow.”
L48@P2: T. S. Eliot, “The Hollow Men,”
L49@P2: Monetary policy deliberations and the actual rate decision are separated by a
L50@P2: “shadow” of persuasion and norms. Decisions by the Federal Open Market Committee
L51@P2: (FOMC) reflect more than macroeconomic data and formal models; they also depend
L52@P2: on members’ experience, behavioral biases, and implicit rules (e.g., Hughes and
L53@P2: Fehrler, 2015; Haldane, 2018; Maih et al., 2021). Consequently, who participates in
L54@P2: the deliberation and how information is communicated can influence policy outcomes
L55@P2: beyond the underlying economic data.
L56@P2: Precisely because of these behavioral forces, traditional models of committee
L57@P2: decision making, though useful and mathematically elegant, often miss the complexities of real world interactions. Behavioral economics highlights how biases, well
L58@P2: documented by Tversky and Kahneman (1974) and shown to affect monetary policy
L59@P2: (Haldane, 2018), can systematically shape decisions. Information design matters too:
L60@P2: Bayesian persuasion demonstrates how agenda setters steer beliefs (Kamenica and
L61@P2: Gentzkow, 2011). Separately, robust control preferences reveal how officials facing
L62@P2: model uncertainty skew choices toward caution (Hansen and Sargent, 2008). Within
L63@P2: the FOMC, policy outcomes depend on the committee’s composition, from regional
L64@P2: voting rotation (e.g., Fos and Xu, 2025) to individual members’ policy leanings (e.g.,
L65@P2: Hack et al., 2023).
L66@P2: To better capture such frictions, researchers increasingly use computational
L67@P2: approaches, such as agent-based models (Dwarakanath et al., 2024) and reinforcement
L68@P2: learning (Hinterlang and Tänzer, 2021). Large language models (LLMs) further
L69@P2: extend the frontier by enabling agents with coherent communication and emergent
L70@P2: behavior. LLM-based generative agents simulate realistic social interactions (Park
L71@P2: et al., 2022) and market dynamics (Zhang et al., 2024), opening new possibilities for
L72@P2: policy experimentation (Argyle et al., 2022; Horton, 2023).
L73@P2: However, no existing approach lets us observe rational and behavioral decision
L74@P2-3: 2rules on the same information set. We address this gap with a dual track simulation
L75@P3: framework that integrates an LLM-driven simulation of the FOMC meeting with a
L76@P3: game theory voting model. In the rational (game theory) track, policymakers observe
L77@P3: macro data, update beliefs via Bayesian inference, and vote to an equilibrium. In the
L78@P3: behavioral (LLM) track, the agents get the same data, reason in natural language,
L79@P3: engage in committee debate, and generate outcomes shaped not only by the data but
L80@P3: also by persona heterogeneity and institutional norms that formal models struggle to
L81@P3: capture. Recent studies show that LLM-based agents can reproduce various aspects
L82@P3: of market dynamics (e.g., Kazinnik, 2023; Manning et al., 2024; Lopez-Lira, 2025);
L83@P3: we apply the same logic to monetary policy. We generalize the Riboni and RugeMurcia (2010) framework to admit heterogeneous preferences, strategic information
L84@P3: disclosure, and a political pressure channel. Deviations between the LLM equilibrium
L85@P3: and the analytic benchmark then isolate the behavioral frictions that standard models
L86@P3: omit.
L87@P3: Specifically, we construct and run two types of simulations: a set of LLMdriven deliberations and a parallel Monte Carlo (MC) analysis. Both start from
L88@P3: the same LLM-generated set of heterogeneous private opinions, reflecting FOMC
L89@P3: members’ profiles and the current economic state. The MC simulation serves as
L90@P3: a statistical baseline, modeling thousands of voting scenarios under theoretical
L91@P3: framework described in Riboni and Ruge-Murcia (2010). The LLM simulation, by
L92@P3: contrast, introduces deliberation, persuasion, and strategic interaction, capturing
L93@P3: human-like dynamics. Comparing the two allows us to isolate and measure the
L94@P3: impact of deliberation by identifying where LLM-driven outcomes diverge from the
L95@P3: statistical baseline.
L96@P3: Within the framework, we start by automatically ingesting real-time macroeconomic data, Governor speeches, district-level reports, and financial news. We
L97@P3: then build detailed profiles for each committee member, combining their historical
L98@P3: policy stances, biographies, recent speeches, district conditions, and the current
L99@P3: macroeconomic context.1 Each agent draws on this information to generate an initial
L100@P3: 1The framework supports introducing new committee members, alternative economic conditions,
L101@P3: and other counterfactual scenarios.
L102@P3-4: 3rate recommendation, comprising a preferred policy rate, a confidence score, and a
L103@P4: short explanation, capturing the agent’s initial belief.
L104@P4: With these agent profiles and initial beliefs in place, we launch the simulation
L105@P4: to model the decision-making process under two approaches. The LLM simulation
L106@P4: begins with several optional rounds of informal coordination to align member views.2
L107@P4: The simulation then enters a deliberation stage, where a discussion engine records
L108@P4: arguments and updates members’ initial beliefs, and concludes with a structured
L109@P4: voting phase in which members submit final rate preferences for automatic aggregation
L110@P4: and comparison. Outputs include posterior beliefs, vote patterns with dissent
L111@P4: diagnostics, and full deliberation logs. The MC framework uses the same priors
L112@P4: and economic parameters but removes conversational and behavioral dynamics,
L113@P4: running thousands of rule-based voting scenarios to generate a statistical baseline.
L114@P4: We benchmark the LLM results against MC ones.
L115@P4: To showcase the framework, we simulate two scenarios. The first one introduces
L116@P4: the effects of a politically charged environment on the committee. This treatment
L117@P4: contains two distinct but related elements, designed to model both the direct pressure
L118@P4: on the current Chair and the indirect, forward-looking behavior of the other committee
L119@P4: members. The first component targets the Chair directly: we apply a dovish bias
L120@P4: in the Chair’s agenda proposal. Simultaneously, the Chair’s institutional authority
L121@P4: is diminished by removing the extra voting weight their ballot typically carries.
L122@P4: The second component of the treatment models the strategic, forward looking
L123@P4: behavior of the other committee members who anticipate an imminent regime change.
L124@P4: Anticipating a more dovishly inclined successor3, members face asymmetric career
L125@P4: incentives, so dissent costs are direction-dependent: hawkish votes carry a higher
L126@P4: penalty, while dovish votes are cheaper, signaling alignment with the expected
L127@P4: regime.4
L128@P4: The second scenario examines the consequences of a sudden negative labor market
L129@P4: data revision. This treatment feeds into the simulation as a downward adjustment

L134@P4: reflecting speculative assessments under a dovish administration based on background, policy views,

L137@P5: uncertainty of employment sensitive members. By modeling this as a real-time
L138@P5: information shock, we capture how the timing and nature of data updates can
L139@P5: meaningfully reshape deliberation and decision making. In our framework, when
L140@P5: members receive new information plays a critical role in shaping the path of discussion,
L141@P5: belief updating, and ultimately, the policy vote.
L142@P5: Our findings are as follows. In the baseline LLM scenario, simulating economic
L143@P5: conditions as of late July 2025 (when the target FFR stood at 4.25%–4.50%, and
L144@P5: effective FFR stood at 4.33%), the committee starts off with a moderately hawkish
L145@P5: tilt, with individual rate preferences spanning 4.20% (for simulated Christopher
L146@P5: Waller, or simWaller) to 4.62% (for simulated Alberto Musalem, or simMusalem)
L147@P5: and clustering at the upper end of the range.5 The average initial recommendation
L148@P5: across members is at 4.375%, with a belief spread of just over 55 basis points. As
L149@P5: deliberations unfold, hawks emphasize the persistence of above-target inflation.6
L150@P5: The committee converges unanimously on a final rate of 4.42%, implying an upward

L152@P5: changing the 4.25%–4.50% range. Parallel Monte Carlo simulations, which remove
L153@P5: conversational dynamics, also converge near the existing range but yield a slightly
L154@P5: lower mean of 4.376%. Outcomes cluster tightly and no dissents occur. Debate thus
L155@P5: introduces a modest hawkish bias of around 5 basis points, relative to rule-based
L156@P5: voting.

L182@P6: Building on this, we introduce a second treatment: a negative labor market data
L183@P6: revision, modeled after the August 1, 2025 Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) release.
L184@P6: This scenario is layered on top of the political pressure context, allowing us to explore
L185@P6: how the shocks compound.7 The data revision enters as a real-time adjustment that
L186@P6: lowers perceived payroll strength and raises uncertainty, especially for employment
L187@P6: sensitive members. In the LLM track, this added shock produces a further drift
L188@P6: downward, albeit small. The average final FFR falls to 4.30%, remaining within the
L189@P6: 4.25%–4.50% range. Dissent, again driven entirely by simWaller, rises to 73% of
L190@P6: simulations. Relative to the baseline, this reflects a 12 basis point easing, consistent
L191@P6: with a softer labor outlook, rather than a major policy regime shift. The MC track
L192@P6: shows a similar downward nudge, with the mean final rate at 4.315% and a standard
L193@P6: deviation of 15 basis points. The median remains at 4.25%, but dissent increases
L194@P6: modestly, averaging 0.62 dissenters per meeting. Taken together, the layering of data
L195@P6: uncertainty on top of political pressure illustrates how these shocks compound, and
L196@P6: showcase how they can amplify disagreement, even within a constrained policy band.
L197@P6: Our work contributes to the intersection of monetary policy committee theory,
L198@P6: behavioral economics, and computational simulation. Building on classic committee
L199@P6: 7Results for a stand-alone data revision shock is in the Online Appendix.
L200@P6-7: 6models (e.g., Gerlach-Kristen, 2006; Riboni and Ruge-Murcia, 2010), we endogenize
L201@P7: persuasion and career incentives by linking them to each member’s information set.
L202@P7: In standard models, influence is imposed exogenously by a chair or agenda setter;
L203@P7: here, influence attempts and their costs arise organically during debate. Unlike
L204@P7: Bayesian persuasion models (e.g., Kamenica and Gentzkow, 2011), which feature
L205@P7: one-to-many communication from a single informed sender, our environment allows
L206@P7: many-to-many strategic exchanges, reflecting the interactive flow of arguments in
L207@P7: actual FOMC meetings. Embedding reputation driven career concerns (Holmström,
L208@P7: 1999) captures how members may adjust their positions to align with current or
L209@P7: anticipated leaders. This creates a novel channel for political pressure on the Chair
L210@P7: to spread: members reposition in anticipation of a leadership change, shifting the
L211@P7: committee’s stance before the change occurs. In sum, our model endogenizes both
L212@P7: persuasion and career incentives, extending committee theory toward a more realistic
L213@P7: representation of decision making.
L214@P7: Second, we link the rational choice committee model to behavioral research
L215@P7: on cognitive biases, transparency, and communication in policy decisions. Prior
L216@P7: work shows that policymakers’ personal experiences can systematically shape their
L217@P7: hawkish or dovish leanings: FOMC members who have lived through high inflation
L218@P7: forecast higher inflation and favor tighter policy, whereas those with benign inflation
L219@P7: histories lean dovish (Malmendier and Nagel, 2016). We embed this experience-based
L220@P7: heterogeneity into our agent profiles, recognizing that members carry distinct biases
L221@P7: and personal histories into deliberations. By integrating these behavioral factors into
L222@P7: a formal voting model, we examine how cognitive biases and institutional features
L223@P7: interact to shape policy outcomes.
L224@P7: Third, our work bridges two rapidly growing strands of computational economics:
L225@P7: agent-based modeling with reinforcement learning for policy design (e.g., Peters
L226@P7: et al., 2022; Cook and Palmer, 2025), and the use of large language model (LLM)
L227@P7: agents to replicate realistic human interaction patterns (e.g., Manning et al., 2024).
L228@P7: Recent studies have begun applying these methods to central banking; for instance,
L229@P7: Seok et al. (2025) simulate deliberative exchanges among LLM agents in stylized
L230@P7: monetary policy settings. Our framework differs in scope and design: we create
L231@P7-8: 7a dual-track environment where deliberative and rational voting behaviors run in
L232@P8: parallel, grounded in real-time macroeconomic data and detailed FOMC member
L233@P8: profiles.
L234@P8: More broadly, this simulation framework provides a controlled environment to
L235@P8: stress test various scenarios. We can experiment in silico (Horton, 2023) with factors
L236@P8: like disclosure rules, dissent penalties, or coalition dynamics to see how they affect
L237@P8: decision making under various scenarios. By enabling counterfactual experimentation
L238@P8: in a realistic setting, this framework lets policymakers and researchers explore various
L239@P8: “what if ” scenarios and observe the possible impacts on committee behavior and
L240@P8: policy.
L241@P8: The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. We review the FOMC meeting
L242@P8: process in Section 2. We then outline our framework in Section 3, including the data
L243@P8: collection, construction of agent personas, the multi-stage simulation design, as well
L244@P8: as the voting process; Section 3.2 describes the game theory implementation and
L245@P8: Section 3.3 describes the Monte Carlo simulation framework. Section 4 explores our
L246@P8: counterfactual scenario and describes the results. Section 5 concludes with some
L247@P8: policy implications.
L248@P8: 2 Modeling FOMC Meetings: Background
L249@P8: “The debate on monetary policy is going on 365 days a year for 24 hours a day, all
L250@P8: around the world. The meetings are definitely important, but they’re a snapshot of the
L251@P8: ongoing debate.”
L252@P8: — Former FOMC member James Bullard, in an interview8
L253@P8: FOMC meetings are highly structured deliberations that anchor U.S. monetary
L254@P8: policy. However, as James Bullard, former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of
L255@P8: St. Louis, suggests, they represent only a moment in time within a broader, ongoing
L256@P8: policy debate. While the meetings formalize key decisions, the underlying policy
L257@P8: dialogue spans months, both within and beyond the Fed.
L258@P8: Each meeting typically follows a fixed agenda: staff economists present updated
L259@P8: 8See Hyatt (2024) for the full interview.
L260@P8-9: 8forecasts and alternative scenarios; FOMC members then offer prepared statements
L261@P9: outlining their interpretations of the data and views on appropriate policy.9 Following
L262@P9: this stage, the Chair opens the floor for discussion, where members respond to others’
L263@P9: arguments, and debate policy options. Finally, the committee votes on the policy
L264@P9: decision. Dissenting votes are relatively rare and, when they occur, serve mainly
L265@P9: to register an alternative viewpoint rather than to overturn the majority consensus
L266@P9: (Thornton and Wheelock, 2014).
L267@P9: Our simulation mirrors the FOMC’s workflow. The sequence of events, the
L268@P9: information available to each participant, and the conversational norms governing
L269@P9: discussion are modeled to reflect actual FOMC dynamics. Because monetary policy
L270@P9: is an ongoing debate rather than a static decision, our framework can continuously

Title: The threat of analytic flexibility in using large language models to simulate human data: A call to attention
Authors: Jamie Cummins
Date: Tue Sep 16 17:29:47 2025

Social scientists are now using large language models to create "silicon samples" - synthetic datasets intended to stand in for human respondents, aimed at revolutionising human subjects research. However, there are many analytic choices which must be made to produce these samples. Though many of these choices are defensible, their impact on sample quality is poorly understood. I map out these analytic choices and demonstrate how a very small number of decisions can dramatically change the correspondence between silicon samples and human data. Configurations (N = 252) varied substantially in their capacity to estimate (i) rank ordering of participants, (ii) response distributions, and (iii) between-scale correlations. Most critically, configurations were not consistent in quality: those that performed well on one dimension often performed poorly on another, implying that there is no "one-size-fits-all" configuration that optimises the accuracy of these samples. I call for greater attention to the threat of analytic flexibility in using silicon samples.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Public opinion polling is seemingly in a crisis (Shapiro 2019). Costs are increasing, response rates are declining (Keeter *et al.* 2017), and there are growing concerns about inaccuracy (Clinton *et al.* 2021a; Clinton, Lapinski, and Trussler 2022; Kennedy *et al.* 2018). At the same time, polls are necessary tools to assess and address growing concerns about polarization and democratic backsliding (Graham 2023; Waldner and Lust 2018). When done well, public opinion polls allow scholars, policymakers, and journalists to assess the opinions of the whole public—not just those who are the most active, willing, and able to express their opinions through more costly means like direct appeals, protests, and donations.

Given the rising expense and difficulty of interviewing respondents, researchers increasingly turn to other methods of characterizing public opinion and sentiment, such as relying on non-survey data (Beauchamp 2017; Tucker 2017) or implementing sophisticated weighting methods (Bisbee 2019; Caughey and Warshaw 2015; Gelman 1997; Ghitza and Gelman 2013; Goplerud 2024; Lax and Phillips 2009).

Large language models (LLMs) that synthesize vast corpora of human-generated text might look like the new frontier in characterizing public opinion without the expense of traditional polling. Social scientists have already used LLMs to label political data (Gilardi, Alizadeh, and Kubli 2023; Törnberg 2023), estimate politicians’ ideology (Wu *et al.* 2023), and generate synthetic samples for pilot testing (Argyle *et al.* 2023; Horton 2023). ## Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) offer new research possibilities for social scientists, but their potential as “synthetic data” is still largely unknown. In this paper, we investigate how accurately the popular LLM ChatGPT can recover public opinion, prompting the LLM to adopt different “personas” and then provide feeling thermometer scores for 11 sociopolitical groups. The average scores generated by ChatGPT correspond closely to the averages in our baseline survey, the 2016–2020 American National Election Study (ANES). Nevertheless, sampling by ChatGPT is not reliable for statistical inference: there is less variation in responses than in the real surveys, and regression coefficients often differ significantly from equivalent estimates obtained using ANES data. We also document how the distribution of synthetic responses varies with minor changes in prompt wording, and we show how the same prompt yields significantly different results over a 3-month period. Altogether, our findings raise serious concerns about the quality, reliability, and reproducibility of synthetic survey data generated by LLMs.

Jamie Cummins

Social scientists are now using large language models to create “silicon samples” - synthetic datasets intended to stand in for human respondents, aimed at revolutionising human subjects research. However, there are many analytic choices which must be made to produce these samples. Though many of these choices are defensible, their impact on sample quality is poorly understood. I map out these analytic choices and demonstrate how a very small number of decisions can dramatically change the correspondence between silicon samples and human data. Configurations (N = 252) varied substantially in their capacity to estimate (i) rank ordering of participants, (ii) response distributions, and (iii) between-scale correlations. Generative large language models (LLMs) have ushered in a sea change within the social sciences. The capacity of these models to produce sensical natural language output to queries, as well as their flexibility, efficiency, and generalisability, has led researchers to explore their use in tasks across the research process. One of the most ambitious proposed uses of LLMs in this respect has been to use them as simulated research participants to determine how human participants might respond to a particular context, set of survey questions, or intervention (Cui et al., 2025). This is based on the tacit assumption that, on some level, the corpuses of data which LLMs are trained on may enable them to approximate similar data-generating processes to those which underpin human responses (Z. Lin, 2025b). If achievable, this could have a transformative impact on the social sciences. It would enable researchers to predict the responses of vulnerable and/or hard-to-reach populations of participants without the need for time- and resource-intensive research studies, improving the representativeness and diversity of research (Sarstedt et al., 2024). --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
